def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover:
## Definition

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternion algebra with its product, its conjugate $x\mapsto\bar x$, its norm $N(x):=x\bar x$, and the inverse $x^{-1}=\bar x/N(x)$ of every nonzero element, in the notation of [[def-quaternions]]. Thus $x=x_0+x_1i+x_2j+x_3k$ with the multiplication formula of [[def-quaternions]], and $N(x)=x_0^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=x\bar x=\bar xx$, with $N(x)>0$ for $x\ne0$ ([[thm-quaternions-form-a-division-ring]]). Under the identification of $\mathbb H$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by the coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_3$ one has $N(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**Imaginary quaternions and the vector identification.** Put

$$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H:=\{x\in\mathbb H:\bar x=-x\}=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk,\qquad \varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H,\quad \varphi(v_1,v_2,v_3):=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k .$$

Then $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism with $N(\varphi(v))=\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. Throughout the collection, $\varphi$ translates between vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ (their inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$, norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ and cross product) and imaginary quaternions inside quaternion products.

**The unit sphere.** Define

$$S^3:=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\},$$

the unit sphere of $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$. The identification of $S^3$ with $SU(2)$ is the one of the published covering example `ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism`, which is also the source of the covering statement recorded in the second remark below; that example is linked from the page summary of this pair.

**Conjugation and the rotation map.** For $q\in\mathbb H$ with $q\ne0$ let $c_q:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ be $c_q(x):=qxq^{-1}=qx\bar q/N(q)$, and define

$$\rho(q):=c_q|_{\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H}:\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H .$$

Both the $\mathbb R$-linear map $\rho(q)$ and its matrix in the ordered basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ are written $\rho(q)$; the equality $\rho(q)\in SO(3)$ for $q\in S^3$ is part of the cited covering statement, and the matrix is the one meant whenever $\rho(q)$ is composed with the identifications above. The map $\rho$ itself is never linear in $q$ and no such structure is used.

**Quaternion lifts.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be a map, with $SO(3)$ as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A **quaternion lift** of $R$ is a map $q:I\to S^3$ with $\rho(q(t))=R(t)$ for every $t\in I$.
lem-cm-quaternion-product-rule-and-conju:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval, let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternions, and let $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ be the identification of [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]].

1. **Product form and product rule.** For $p=s+\varphi(u)$ and $q=t+\varphi(w)$ with $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u,w\in\mathbb R^3$ one has $pq=\bigl(st-\langle u,w\rangle_2\bigr)+\varphi\bigl(sw+tu+u\times w\bigr)$. If moreover $p,q:I\to\mathbb H$ are of class $C^1$ (componentwise, [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), then $pq:I\to\mathbb H$ is $C^1$ and $(pq)'=p'q+pq'$. Likewise, if $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ are of class $C^1$, then $AB$ is $C^1$ and $(AB)'=A'B+AB'$.
2. **Conjugation and norm.** For all $p,q\in\mathbb H$ one has $\overline{pq}=\bar q\,\bar p$ and $N(pq)=N(p)N(q)$, and $\operatorname{Re}(p\bar q)=\langle p,q\rangle_2$ for $\operatorname{Re}(x):=x_0$ and the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For a $C^1$ curve $q:I\to\mathbb H$, the curves $\bar q$ and $N\circ q$ are $C^1$ with $\overline{q}'=\overline{q'}$ and

$$(N\circ q)'=2\operatorname{Re}(q'\bar q)=2\langle q',q\rangle_2 .$$

3. **Conjugation formula.** If $q=a+\varphi(u)$ with $a\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$, and $v\in\mathbb R^3$, then

$$q\,\varphi(v)\,\bar q=\varphi\Bigl((a^2-\|u\|_2^2)\,v+2\langle u,v\rangle_2\,u+2a\,(u\times v)\Bigr);$$

in particular $q\,\varphi(v)\,\bar q$ is imaginary for every $q\in\mathbb H$, that is, its real part is $0$.
4. **Axis-angle form.** If $N(q)=1$ and $q=\cos(\theta/2)+\varphi(\hat n)\sin(\theta/2)$ with $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\hat n\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|\hat n\|_2=1$, then for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$

$$\rho(q)\bigl(\varphi(v)\bigr)=\varphi\Bigl(\cos\theta\,v+(1-\cos\theta)\langle \hat n,v\rangle_2\,\hat n+\sin\theta\,(\hat n\times v)\Bigr).$$
lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotati:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $SO(3)$ be as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]], and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be of class $C^1$, that is, all nine entries of $R$ have continuous first derivatives; write $R'(t)$ for the entrywise derivative and put

$$\Omega(t):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)\in M_3(\mathbb R)$$

for the product of the transpose of $R(t)$ with $R'(t)$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-matrix-space]]). Then:

1. $\Omega(t)$ is skew-symmetric for every $t\in I$, that is $\Omega(t)^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega(t)$.
2. There is exactly one map $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)\,z=\omega(t)\times z\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^3,\ t\in I),$$

namely $\omega(t)=\bigl(-\Omega_{23}(t),\ \Omega_{13}(t),\ -\Omega_{12}(t)\bigr)$, and this $\omega$ is continuous. It is called the **body angular velocity** of $R$.
3. For every $t\in I$, writing $\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for the matrix $z\mapsto\omega(t)\times z$, one has $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$.
lem-cm-quaternion-lift-of-a-prescribed-b:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, and consider on $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$ the initial value problem

$$q'(t)=\tfrac12\,q(t)\,\varphi\bigl(\omega(t)\bigr),\qquad q(t_0)=q_0,$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with state domain $U=\mathbb H$ and right-hand side $F(t,q)=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, where $\varphi$, $S^3$ and $\rho$ are those of [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]].

1. If $q:I\to\mathbb H$ is a $C^1$ solution of $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, then $N\circ q$ is constant on $I$; if $q(t_0)\in S^3$ for one $t_0\in I$, then $q(I)\subseteq S^3$ and the curve

$$R:=\rho\circ q:I\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=\rho(q(t)),$$

is of class $C^1$ with $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for every $t\in I$; consequently $\omega$ is the body angular velocity of $R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]].
2. For every $t_0\in I$ and $q_0\in S^3$ the problem has exactly one maximal solution, and its domain is all of $I$; that is, there is exactly one $C^1$ curve $q:I\to S^3$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$ and $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$ on $I$, and clause 1 applies to it.
prop-cm-quaternion-angular-velocity-reco:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $q:I\to S^3$ be of class $C^1$, and let

$$R:I\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=\rho(q(t)),$$

be the associated rotation path, the matrix being taken in the basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ ([[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]]). Then:

1. $q(t)^{-1}q'(t)=\bar q(t)q'(t)$ has real part $0$ for every $t\in I$, so there is a unique vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with

$$q(t)^{-1}q'(t)=\tfrac12\,\varphi\bigl(\omega(t)\bigr),$$

namely $\omega(t)=2\operatorname{Im}\bigl(q(t)^{-1}q'(t)\bigr)$, and $t\mapsto\omega(t)$ is continuous.
2. The curve $q$ solves $q'(t)=\tfrac12q(t)\,\varphi(\omega(t))$ on $I$, the matrix curve $R$ is of class $C^1$, and $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for every $t\in I$, where $\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ is the matrix $z\mapsto\omega(t)\times z$.
3. Consequently $\omega$ is the body angular velocity of $R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]]: $R$ is a $C^1$ rotation path whose body angular velocity is $\omega$.
thm-cm-quaternion-lift-exists-and-is-uni:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) with body angular velocity $\omega_R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]], let $t_0\in I$, and let $q_0\in S^3$ satisfy $\rho(q_0)=R(t_0)$, with $\rho$ and $S^3$ as in [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]]. Then:

1. There is exactly one $C^1$ quaternion lift $q:I\to S^3$ of $R$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$, namely the unique solution on $I$ of the initial value problem

$$q'(t)=\tfrac12\,q(t)\,\varphi\bigl(\omega_R(t)\bigr),\qquad q(t_0)=q_0 .$$

2. Every $C^1$ lift $\tilde q:I\to S^3$ of $R$ satisfies $\tilde q=q$ or $\tilde q=-q$; in particular $-q$ is the lift with initial value $-q_0$, and $\rho\circ q=\rho\circ(-q)=R$.
rem-cm-quaternion-lift-scope-and-sign:
## Statement

The following qualifications are part of what the preceding items do and do not claim.

1. **Two lifts and one rotation.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be of class $C^1$. By [[thm-cm-quaternion-lift-exists-and-is-unique]], $R$ has exactly two $C^1$ quaternion lifts, namely $q$ and $-q$ for any one lift $q$, both solve $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega_R(t))$ for the same body angular velocity $\omega_R$, and $\rho(q)=\rho(-q)=R$. By the scaling recorded in [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]], $\rho(\lambda q)=\rho(q)$ for every $\lambda\ne0$, so a rotation is represented by the antipodal pair $\pm q$ of unit quaternions and by no other data of the quaternion itself.

2. **No globally continuous sign choice.** The sign of a lift is not determined by $R$, and the two signs cannot always be glued continuously along closed motion. The companion examples page proves exactly this in finite form: it exhibits a $C^1$ closed loop $R:[0,1]\to SO(3)$ with $R(0)=R(1)=I$ whose unique $C^1$ lift through $q(0)=1$ ends at $q(1)=-1$, so that closed loop admits no closed $C^1$ lift through $1$; the explicit item is linked in the Remarks below. In this sense the sign ambiguity is intrinsic and not an artifact of the formula $\rho(q)(x)=qxq^{-1}$.

3. **No physical claim.** Every statement on this page concerns curves into $S^3$ and into the matrix group $SO(3)$ and the differential equation $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$. No quantum-mechanical spin, relativistic, or half-integer-angular-momentum interpretation is asserted, no measurement is reported, and no empirical precision is claimed anywhere.
